title: The Limoncello Spritz Is Euro Summer in a Glass
summary:
Limoncello is having a long-overdue renaissance, and the liqueur is starring in spritzes all across Italy and beyond.

The post The Limoncello Spritz Is Euro Summer in a Glass appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
As far as Italian institutions go, limoncello is relatively new. While its precise origins are unknown and somewhat contested—the Gulf of Naples, Amalfi Coast, and Sicily all claim bragging rights—the sweet, highly alcoholic lemon liqueur was likely invented in the early 20th century, growing in popularity until it became one of the most famous ways to end a long, leisurely Italian meal. (Grappa, another iconic Italian liqueur, dates back to the 14th century.) 

Even as the citrus digestif became known nationally and around the world, limoncello remained largely artisanal, with families throughout Southern Italy taking pride in their recipes and lemons. But industrialized, cloyingly sweet limoncellos made with less-than-fresh lemons have proliferated too, souring the drink’s reputation.

Now, a new wave of producers and drink makers are giving limoncello the respect it deserves—in cocktail form. Traditionally sipped or taken as a shot after dinner, limoncello is less known as an ingredient in mixed libations. But that’s changing, largely because of one drink in particular: the spritz.

The light, sunny limoncello spritz is currently one of the hottest cocktails in Italy, particularly in regions known for their lemons, like Amalfi and Capri. This summer at Pazziella, a Luxury Collection Hotel in Capri, the cocktail has become so popular that bartender Marco Gunetti created a “Limoncello Spritz Ritual,” offering guests a guided tasting of three different variations, with Gunetti providing tips for preparing them at home.

What makes these spritzes so special are the local lemons that produce the limoncello—a draw for tourists increasingly geared towards terroir and regional authenticity. “Capri lemons are a true expression of their unique territory,” says Gunetti. “The island’s mild climate, sea breeze, and mineral-rich soil give the fruit an exceptionally intense aroma and a peel naturally rich in essential oils.”

The Limoncello Renaissance

Beyond Capri and across Italy, the liqueur is trending, in part thanks to their spritz potential.

“Limoncello is definitely having a renaissance right now,” says Alessandro Buonadonna, head barman and mixologist director at Grand Hotel Villa Serbelloni on Lake Como. It’s increasingly playing a starring role in spritzes, which themselves are on the upswing. The limoncello spritz is made with the lemon liqueur, Prosecco, club soda, and mint leaves.

Buonadonna attributes the limoncello spritz’s popularity to its simplicity and the fruity synchronicity “of both Prosecco and limoncello, which leaves a delightful taste without dryness.” Heavy on its own, limoncello really shines with some dilution. “The citrusy kick of limoncello adds a vibrant and refreshing twist to the spritz,” he says. 

To make the drink at J.K. Place Capri, located in one of the great limoncello capitals of Italy, assistant restaurant manager Vincenzo Nappi insists upon using all-natural Limoncello di Capri, which is produced only with regionally certified Sorrento lemon peels, alcohol, water, and sugar. 

Although limoncello hails from many regions in Italy, he swears by bottles from the Sorrento coast made with artisanal methods that “respect the traditions and flavors of the island of Capri.” Sometimes Nappi will even modify the drink with strawberries to make a limoncello spritz rosso, which delivers a lovely pink hue.

On the nearby Amalfi coast, Hotel Poseidon Positano is also well-known for its limoncello spritz, which is made with limoncello produced via a treasured family recipe. “It works so well in a cocktail, particularly on warmer days, as it’s reminiscent of a lemon sorbet,” says Liliana Mascolo, one of the family members who owns and runs the hotel. “It’s refreshing and a little tart, with just the right amount of sweetness.”

Because it’s so unfussy, the limoncello spritz is an ideal summer cocktail to make at home. That said, each ingredient requires proper attention because there are so few. For the Prosecco, Buonadonna recommends a bubbly like Jeio by Bisol, an extra-dry bottle with “a fragrant and fruity nature that complements the citrus flavors of limoncello.” 

Choosing the Right Limoncello

As for the limoncello, there is no shortage of excellent options. “When choosing a limoncello, it is important to focus on the producers, and there are a few very interesting ones who have come along recently,” says Nicola Spaggiari, bar manager at Borgo Santo Pietro in Tuscany. These days, Spaggiara likes limoncello from Villa Massa, a Sorrento-based producer that uses hand-picked lemons, and Assuntina, a maker out of Capri that uses underripe lemons to make a bright-green limoncello.

Buonadonna is currently excited about Distilleria Cioffi, a producer based in Ravello, on the Amalfi Coast, which employs traditional methods like harvesting the lemons at dawn, at the peak of their flavor. The resulting flavor profile is “balanced, soft, and sweet, with a long, juicy citrus consistency,” Buonadonna says.

The renaissance has even migrated out of the south and across Italy, to places where limoncello traditionally has not been made. Scuppoz, one of Spaggiari’s favorite producers, is based in Abruzzo. Their limoncello is made with lemons grown on the Adriatic Coast, which offer a less-sweet profile than what you’ll find in Amalfi (and a higher alcohol content). 

The thirst for limoncello spritzes will only continue to grow, says Spaggiari, who is based in Tuscany, because it’s the perfect way to enjoy a traditional Italian product in the refreshing spritz format. But you don’t have to travel to Italy to drink it—just make the following recipe at home.

How to Make a Limoncello Spritz

Recipe courtesy of Hotel Poseidon Positano

  • 1 ⅔ ounces (50 ml) limoncello (such as Limoncello di Capri)
  • 2 ½ ounces (75 ml) Prosecco
  • ¾ ounces (25 ml) soda water
Step 1
Fill a long glass, ideally a wine or hurricane glass, with ice.
Step 2
Pour all the ingredients into the glass in the following order: limoncello, Prosecco, soda water.
Step 3
Stir well with a long spoon.
Step 4
Decorate with a lime or lemon slice and cherries.

title: Emidio Pepe’s Winemaking Ideas Were Old-Fashioned, Until They Were Radical
summary:
One day after his 94th birthday, the world lost an Italian wine legend who refused to modernize what didn't need improving.

The post Emidio Pepe’s Winemaking Ideas Were Old-Fashioned, Until They Were Radical appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
When Emidio Pepe began bottling wine in Abruzzo in 1964, the Italian wine industry was heading rapidly in another direction. Stainless steel, mechanization, and modern enology promised cleaner, more consistent wines and a path toward the international market. He chose to remain true to himself, and his region.

Pepe, who died on July 28, one day after turning 94, would later be described as a pioneer of biodynamic and even natural wine. But perhaps his greater significance was that he remained a living bridge between two Italys: the agricultural world he was born into and the modern wine country that developed around him.

A Relic of a Kinder Past

Throughout his illustrious career, Pepe kept farming and making wine much as it had been done before industrialization. At his eponymous winery, vineyards were worked by hand and without synthetic chemicals. Whites were crushed by foot, reds destemmed by hand, and fermentations occurred spontaneously in glass-lined concrete, without filtration or added sulfites.

When I visited Pepe in Abruzzo in 2019, the language barrier meant we spoke little. Since he was already retired, his granddaughter Chiara de Iulis Pepe hosted me. But in some ways, watching him told me more. In his coppola (flat cap) and groomed mustache, moving through the rhythms of the day and, after lunch, sitting down with the newspaper, he seemed rooted in another era, shaped by vineyard work, meals, family, and familiar rituals. It was genuinely how he lived.

Perhaps that is what made Pepe so unusual. He never saw a reason to abandon the parts of tradition that worked.

That same stubborn continuity defined his wines. Pepe found a kindred spirit in Luigi Veronelli, the influential Italian writer who championed small farmers and believed wine should be cultivated, not manufactured. After Veronelli’s death, Chiara recalled one of the beliefs he and Pepe shared: “The smaller the estate, the tinier the vineyard, the more perfect the wine.”

That faith mattered in Abruzzo, where Montepulciano was largely sold in bulk or drunk locally. Starting with just 1.5 hectares, Pepe believed Montepulciano and Trebbiano could make profound, long-lived wines, a conviction that initially raised eyebrows even within his family.

Time vindicated him beautifully. From Veronelli’s legendary cellar, I tasted Pepe’s 1975 Montepulciano, still remarkably alive. Later, I bought his 1971 Trebbiano from the same collection. More than half a century after harvest, it was one of the finest bottles of white wine I have ever tasted: living proof that Pepe was ahead of his time.

And what once appeared old-fashioned eventually became radical again.

Ahead of ‘Natural Wine’

I saw that reversal firsthand three years before my visit to Abruzzo. In 2016, as New York’s natural wine scene was exploding, I attended Big Glou in Williamsburg. Among a young crowd excited about low-intervention winemaking were Pepe’s granddaughters, Chiara and Elisa, pouring wines made according to principles their grandfather had followed for more than half a century.

The irony was striking. Pepe hadn’t adapted to natural wine. It was the hipsters that just labeled his old-school approach as “natural.”

Time proved him right. Pepe routinely held back half of each vintage, sometimes much more. Over the years, his cellar became an archive of his convictions, vintage after vintage proving that Abruzzo’s native grapes possessed a longevity few had imagined.

“He lived an absolutely incredible life, full of all things,” Chiara told me after his death. “He felt he had to prove himself his whole life and towards the end he got the moral recognition he was looking for.”

By then, the wine world had changed around him, only to circle back toward ideas he had never abandoned. Chiara’s memories also revealed a man of simple pleasures: dancing the waltz, growing tomatoes, pruning fruit trees, eating spaghetti, driving his tractor, and, unexpectedly, enjoying New York street food. Perhaps they were all part of the same philosophy: to live closely, patiently, and with little concern for fashion.

His daughters, Sofia and Daniela, as well as his granddaughters, now carry that life’s work forward. “We feel the privilege to have had him in our lives and to have learnt from him,” Chiara said. “We will work relentlessly to honor the legacy he has left us.”

With Pepe’s death, Italian wine loses more than one of its great growers. It loses one of its last direct links to a world before wine became an industry, when the farmer, the vineyard, and the cellar were not separate ideas.

Emidio Pepe spent his life refusing to modernize what he believed didn’t need improving. In the end, modern wine came back around to him.

How Boisset Collection Celebrates the Bond Between French and American Winemaking

While companies devoted to championing Burgundian and Californian wines, respectively, are quick to debate what makes each region so nuanced and singular, few truly celebrate the deep link between French and American winemaking traditions and culture. For over five decades, family-owned Boisset Collection has successfully brought together more than 30 legendary wineries across California and Burgundy, as well as from Beaujolais, the Rhône Valley, and the South of France that share over 7,000 years of history.

As America celebrates its 250th anniversary, it’s an especially compelling time to reflect on the historic relationship that binds the two countries together.

By uniting iconic Burgundian names like Bouchard Aîné & Fils and Domaine de la Vougeraie to Californian icons like Buena Vista Winery, Raymond Vineyards, DeLoach Vineyards, and Elizabeth Spencer, Boisset cemented its position as one of the leading luxury names in Franco-American wine.

Additionally, Boisset Collection is a household name for prestige sparkling wines, including JCB Jean-Charles Boisset Crémant de Bourgogne and Champagne. 

Beyond a commitment to preserving each winery within its portfolio’s lasting legacy and heritage, the company’s focus on sustainability in farming and production has helped bring each estate proudly into the 21st century. 

Founder Jean-Charles Boisset personally initiated the implementation of biodynamic farming at all of the family’s estates. Boisset’s first estate vineyard in California, DeLoach Vineyards in Sonoma’s Russian River Valley is a renowned producer of Chardonnay, Zinfandel, and Pinot Noir, and it began its estate transition to regenerative agriculture in 2004.

Four years later, the winery received an organic seal of approval by California Certification of Organic Farmers (CCOF) and earned a biodynamic certification by Demeter just two years later. To mark its 50th anniversary vintage of Pinot Noir this year, DeLoach’s $50 bottles bear the label, “Made With Organic Grapes.”

Similarly, Raymond Vineyards was also certified CCOF and Demeter in 2013, making it the largest certified biodynamic estate on the Napa Valley floor. In accordance with the Demeter Biodynamic Farm Standard, Raymond set aside 10% of its estate to biodiversity, including the Theater of Nature, Napa Valley’s most comprehensive, interactive tour of biodynamic farming.

According to utility provider Blue Sky Utility, Raymond Vineyards is now the largest 100% solar-powered winery in Napa, boasting more than 50,000 square feet of panels on the winery’s roofs and a 17,000 square foot solar canopy.  

Boisset Collection’s commitment to sustainability crosses both sides of the pond. This stewardship and love of the land hails from the family’s deep roots in the French wine industry.

Born in the village of Vougeot, Jean-Charles’ passion for wine began as a child. He grew up above the cellars and within view of the centuries-old vineyards of Château du Clos de Vougeot, the epicenter and birthplace of Pinot Noir and Chardonnay.

His parents, Jean-Claude and Claudine, founded the family winery in 1961.

But it wasn’t until 1999 that Jean-Charles and his sister Nathalie teamed up to unite the family’s Burgundy vineyards, including prestigious monopoles such as the Vougeot 1er Cru Clos Blanc de Vougeot—planted in 1110 by the Cistercian monks—into what is now one of Burgundy’s leading domaines.

Domaine de la Vougeraie has been using biodynamic cultivation methods since its creation in 1999. As the leading organic and biodynamic domaine in the Côte d’Or, Domaine de la Vougeraie has more than 95 acres under cultivation.

Whether you’re looking to elevate a celebratory dinner paired with a top producer of Burgundian Pinot Noir or Napa Valley Cabernet Sauvignon, or mark a special occasion with a world-class bottle of bubbly, look to Boisset Collection for exceptional quality and care.

title: The Next ‘White Lotus’ Locale Is a Glitzy Rosé Paradise. Here’s Where Insiders Go
summary:
Shop like a costumer, party like the rich and famous, and drink some of the best rosé on the planet in the charming Côte d'Azur village.

The post The Next ‘White Lotus’ Locale Is a Glitzy Rosé Paradise. Here’s Where Insiders Go appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
Must-Visit Stops
  • Place des Lices — Browse lively markets, watch pétanque games, and experience authentic village life.
  • Le Tarte Tropézienne — Taste the town’s signature cream-filled brioche at its original bakery.
  • Café Sénéquier — Harborfront institution for rosé, people-watching, and classic French café fare.
  • Byblos Beach — Glamorous beach club combining celebrity appeal, Provençal cuisine, and al fresco dining.
Wineries
  • Château Minuty — Provence’s iconic rosé estate, with sweeping vineyard views above the Gulf of Saint-Tropez.
  • Château Barbeyrolles — Family-run biodynamic vineyard offering intimate tastings paired with local goat cheese.
  • Bertaud Belieu — Elegant winery known for acclaimed Heraklion wines and cheese-paired tastings.
Eat & Drink
  • Le Girelier — Order salt-crusted sea bass or bouillabaisse overlooking Saint-Tropez’s glamorous marina.
  • Le Belrose — Michelin-recommended Mediterranean dining with panoramic sunset views and exceptional regional wines.
  • Beefbar — Premium steaks, inventive tapas, and stylish terrace dining overlooking the pool.
  • Zuma — Sophisticated Japanese cuisine featuring robata grilling and signature seafood dishes.
Shop
  • Rondini & K.Jacques — Handmade Tropezian leather sandals crafted by the town’s iconic artisans.
  • Bla-Bla — Mediterranean-inspired resortwear favored by White Lotus costume designers.
  • By Marie — Refined beachwear and elegant accessories capture Saint-Tropez’s effortless, understated Riviera style.
Nightlife
  • Le Café — Live music, polished brasserie classics, and an excellent wine list on Place des Lices.
  • L’Opéra — Dinner theater transforms into one of Saint-Tropez’s signature late-night party spots.
  • Les Caves du Roy — Legendary nightclub with celebrity clientele since the 1960s.
Outdoors
  • Cap Taillat — Protected peninsula with crystal-clear water, scenic hikes, paddleboarding, and catamaran cruises.
  • Sentier du Littoral — Coastal trail revealing secluded coves, villas, and Pampelonne Beach beyond the crowds.
Stay
  • Hôtel Byblos — Legendary celebrity hotel with refreshed rooms, rooftop cocktails, and impeccable service.
  • Hôtel Lou Pinet — Design-forward retreat with the area’s largest hotel pool and relaxed bohemian style.
  • Althoff Villa Belrose — Perched above Saint-Tropez, this tranquil five-star retreat pairs panoramic bay views with elegant rooms, a cliffside pool, and easy access to town.
  • Château de La Messardière — White Lotus filming location offering palace luxury and panoramic bay views.

Ever since Brigitte Bardot and the 1956 film And God Created Woman catapulted Saint-Tropez into international fame, the former fishing village has been a magnet for celebrities and global jet setters, establishing its reputation as an ultra-exclusive summer escape. 

This year, the spotlight is shining even brighter than usual, thanks to 1% satire White Lotus. Filming for season four is underway at Château de La Messardière, a 19th-century palace-turned-hotel on the edge of town. 

“There’s definitely been a buzz,” says Antoine Chevanne, owner of the iconic Hôtel Byblos. “Saint-Tropez always has energy in high season, but there’s been extra excitement and curiosity with the production in the region.”

Sought-after destinations have been fully packed with visitors seeking to get in on the action. “Byblos is fully booked, more than ever,” he adds. “The hotel always is, of course, but this year the surge has spilled into our restaurants, bars, and beach club.”

Kimberley Cohen, co-founder and artistic director of boutique hotel collection Maisons Pariente, has seen a similar trend this year. “There’s a wonderful energy throughout the village, with a truly international crowd and a real appetite for discovering new places alongside the iconic ones,” she says. “At Lou Pinet we’ve watched guests settle in and savor the hotel itself rather than rushing from one address to another. Evenings in particular have had a wonderful energy, with Beefbar drawing an especially lively crowd as the sun goes down.”

Whether you’re seeking to hole up at one of the town’s luxe hotels like the White Lotus guests, taste iconic rosės at idyllic vineyards, shop like a costume designer, or take in the natural beauty that made the village such a popular destination in the first place, book a trip to Côte d’Azur village stat. Here are the top things to eat, drink, do, and where to stay in St. Tropez.

Sip Provence’s Best Rosé In Situ

There are dozens of vineyards on the Cap de Saint-Tropez, each with their own merits and takes on regional wines. Château Minuty is perhaps the most famous, which is probably why luxury powerhouse LVMH bought it from the marketing savvy Matton family in 2023. It is also one of the oldest vineyards on the peninsula, founded in 1936. Perched on the hillsides of Gassin and Ramatuelle villages, the nearly 500-acre-estate overlooks the bright blue waters of the Gulf of Saint-Tropez and its surrounding Massif des Maures mountain range. “The property is very beautiful and has a very sweet little chapel where the Matton family used to hold weddings and baptisms,” says Robert van Straaten, general manager of five-star hotel Althoff Villa Belrose in nearby Gassin. 

Just down the street, the 12-acre, family-owned vineyard Château Barbeyrolles organically and, on some plots, biodynamically farm the region’s signature red and white grapes, which are hand-harvested and vinified via gravity with indigenous yeasts. Multiple tasting options are available including a discovery tasting of three wines (red, white, and rosé) that requires no reservation and 90-minute tours and tastings of five wines accompanied by goat cheese.

A five-minute drive away, Bertaud Belieu is a stunning property and venue that has hosted many high-end events, including the annual Leonardo DiCaprio Foundation gala. Rows of green vines surround the terracotta-roofed winery and tasting room with its grand Neoclassical columns and pediments. It’s not only a beautiful place to spend time, but “they make excellent rosé, white, and red wines,” van Straaten adds. “The Heraklion wines, in particular, are very special.”

Guests can taste through the lineup with one-and-a-half hour tastings, paired cheese and charcuterie, five days a week starting at 10 am. Reservations are required.

Live (Near) the Yacht Life at Harborview Restaurants

There’s a reason Cafe Sénéquier frequently gets mentioned as one of the must-visit spots in Saint-Tropez. The circa-1930 café started as a pastry shop before transforming into the bustling café it is today. In addition to breakfast, lunch, and dinner bistro mainstays like omelettes, escargot, and beef béarnaise, guests can sip signature cocktails, spritzes, and a large selection of wines. 

“It’s the perfect spot to watch people and boats while sipping a glass of chilled rosé,” says Marianne Fabre-Lanvin, founder of Souleil Wines. “The wine list features local gems, including rosé of course, as well as fine whites from Côtes de Provence, Palette, Cassis, and Bandol for example.”

Down the harbor Le Girelier is another “must-visit spot at the port of Saint-Tropez, with an elegant setting, design, and décor reminiscent of the yachting world, plus impeccable service,” says Adélie Ferrari of Château Malherbe in nearby Bormes-les-Mimosas. She recommends ordering the “whole sea bream or sea bass, without hesitation—especially in a salt crust, it’s even better,” she says. “Otherwise, the bouillabaisse, the local specialty.”

For a bird’s eye view of the harbor and town, head to the terrace of Le Belrose restaurant. The Michelin-recommended Mediterranean spot is set in the hills of Gassin on the property of Althoff Villa Belrose, offering incredible sunsets if you time it right. Either way, the scenery is spectacular, and chef Jimmy Coutel’s upscale regional cuisine is worth the splurge. Anticipate options like razor clams and Baeri caviar and lamb stuffed with black olive compote, eggplant, chanterelles, garlic potato mousseline, and wild thyme jus. Make sure to explore the extensive wine list for hard-to-find local reds or whites, made from regionally-approved varietals such as Grenache, Syrah, Mourvèdre, Rolle (Vermentino), Ugni Blanc, and Clairette.

Stroll the Streets for Snacks

A big part of what makes St. Tropez so iconic is the pastel-colored buildings lining the streets. A walk through town is a must, says Olivier Souvelain, general manager at Château Gassier in the heart of Provence: “Soak in the charm of its boutiques, the postcard-perfect harbor and bell tower, and the colorful local market on Place des Lices.”

Home to the Tuesday and Saturday markets, Place des Lices is the town’s central hub. Back in the day, Bardot would take it over to throw massive parties. Today, locals gather there in the late afternoon to play jeu de boule, a game with big heavy steel balls that’s similar to bocce. The association Les Boules Tropezienne organizes regular tournaments.

On many evenings when she’s in town, Cohen heads there to listen to the street musicians perform, “as the village comes alive after sunset,” she says. “It’s one of my favorite moments.”

She also highly recommends hitting up the markets (as well as the Sunday market in Ramatuelle). “Beyond shopping for a beautiful pareo, handmade ceramics, olive oil, or fresh flowers, they’re where you really feel the rhythm of local life,” she says.

Catty corner to the plaza is the original location of legendary Bardot-approved institution Le Tarte Tropézienne. The bakery is where the iconic pastry of the same name was created, made with a top secret recipe (which is actually locked up in a safe) of orange blossom- or vanilla-scented pastry cream sandwiched between a sweet brioche. 

It’s a must-try, but “for something a little more discreet but equally memorable, I always recommend the apple tarte fine at Les Deux Frères,” says Cohen. “It’s beautifully simple and one of those little pleasures I look forward to every summer.”

The bakery is a local favorite for croissants, pain au chocolat, baguettes, and just about every other French boulangerie staple. Van Straaten suggests grabbing a pastry from there and taking it to Quartier La Ponche, a historic neighborhood near the water, or the end of the harbor to enjoy a treat with a view. 

And, if you want to dig deep into wine, Fabre-Lanvin suggests checking out Cave 1990. “It’s a fantastic local wine shop with a carefully selected collection and passionate, knowledgeable staff,” she says. “Bonus: they’ll deliver right to your boat”—if you just so happen to have one docked in the area.”

Shop Like a Tropizien

There are numerous luxury storefronts spread throughout the streets, including an iconic Chanel outpost located in an old hotel and a Dior boutique in a historic town house with a little garden. But “you have to walk through La Rue Clemenceau to the harbor and visit Rondini for real Tropezian handmade leather sandals and other beautiful shops like Marinette for Provençal napkins, table clothes, and cushions,” says van Straaten.

If you want to dress like White Lotus’s now-deceased Tonya McQuoid, check out local boutiques where the show’s customers have been outfitting Laura Dern, Rosie Perez, and other cast members. They’ve been hitting Bla-Bla on Rue François Sibilli for caftans, sun hats, and Mediterranean-inspired wares.

In that vein, Cohen, who started off her career working in fashion, loves recommending “boutiques that capture the effortless elegance of Saint-Tropez,” she says. “By Marie is perfect for refined beachwear and accessories, K.Jacques is a timeless institution for handcrafted leather sandals, and Battaglia offers beautiful vintage pieces.”

Dine Then Dance

After hitting the shops, grab a table at Le Café. Set on Place des Lices, the restaurant boasts “wonderful ambiance, including live music in the evening,” says van Straaten. The international menu overseen by Eric Frechon, who worked in three-Michelin-star restaurants in Paris, features brasserie-style fare with Mediterranean accents such as baked mussels, sole Meunière with lemon confit, and ricotta ravioli with black truffle. Plus, “they have a very good wine list and excellent service,” van Straaten adds.

Around the corner, Cohen recommends Pablo “for dinner that naturally turns into an evening out.” The restaurant is known for its ice cold tequila cocktails, Mexican tapas, and overall sensual vibe.

L’Opéra on the harbor is known for its international cocktails, big Champagne bottles, sexy dinner show, and late-night dancing. For some potential celeb sightings while clubbing, head to Les Caves du Roy at the Hôtel Byblos. Since it first opened in 1967, it’s been known worldwide for its distinctive illuminated palm trees, high-energy music, and celebrity clientele that spans from Mick Jagger, Grace Jones, and Elton John to Paris Hilton, Lady Gaga, and Jay-Z.

Get Outdoors

After a late night, enjoy the outdoors by booking a table at Byblos Beach “for a stylish toes-in-the-sand day,” Ferrari says. The infamous beach club attracts the same celebrities as the infamous hotel and its nightclub, including George Clooney, Leonardo DiCaprio, Beyoncé, and Mick Jagger. Known for its sexy vibe and locally-sourced cuisine (some of which comes from its own permaculture garden), the Ramatuelle restaurant offers international fare like yellowtail tiradito, linguine with clams, and Provençal aioli with local fish and vegetables right next to the sand. 

If you want to do more than lounge in a beach chair after lunch, consider “stopping by the Club 55 boutique, which has a wonderful selection of resortwear and beach essentials,” says Cohen. 

If you’d like to burn some calories, she recommends renting an electric bike to explore the hills above Ramatuelle. “Stop along the way to admire the breathtaking views over Pampelonne Bay and discover the region’s iconic windmills,” says Cohen.

Or, sweat out the rosé at Cap Taillat. The secluded natural escape is less than a 30-minute drive from Byblos Beach and offers crystal clear waters and incredible views of the other two capes and the Hyères island. “Cap Taillat is one of the last preserved and natural spots in the Saint-Tropez area, near Ramatuelle,” says Souvelain. “Apart from walking around, wandering, and enjoying the scenery, there’s not much else to do—this is what’s so special about it.”

Though, if you really need something to do, paddleboard rentals are available, as are catamaran cruises. 

Back near town, Cohen suggests waking up early for a morning walk down Sentier du Littoral before the day heats up. The hiking path starts near the pier and passes along crystal clear waters through the maritime cemetery where Bardot and director Roger Vadim are buried, stunning villas, and multiple sandy stretches before ending at the popular Plage de Pampelonne beach. “It reveals a completely different side of the peninsula: wild, peaceful, and almost meditative,” she says.

For an easier nature excursion, walk through Citadelle de Saint-Tropez. The historic 17th-century fortress boasts a museum with nautical exhibits and a scenic roof terrace, but it’s also a beautiful place to escape the hordes and burn some calories while admiring coastal views.

Go Beyond French Fare

While Mediterranean and French fare rule the roost in Saint-Tropez, this internationally-visited village also offers international cuisines. 

Beefbar, an outpost of the Monaco temple of meat, offers prime cuts of wagyu, Black Angus, and other steaks paired with South American- and Asian-inspired tapas like Japanese Kobe gyoza and the guest-favorite tempura-fried rock corn. Book a table on the beautiful terrace that overlooks the hotel pool. Make sure to try one of the excellent cocktails from the bar.

“For a chic, modern take on Japanese cuisine,” Ferrari suggests heading to the local outpost of Zuma. Set in the base of Hôtel Byblos, the upscale izakaya offers a solid selection of sushi, robata-grilled meats, and signature plates, like roasted lobster with green chilli and garlic shiso butter.

Also in the famed hotel, recently opened Il Giardino offers classic Italian fare, like decadent seafood pasta and T-bone all Fiorentina, with an extensive Italian wine list on a plant-covered poolside pergola. Make sure to save room for the ice cream cart with instant vanilla and lemon ice cream made tableside with an impressive selection of gourmet toppings.

Luna Rossa on Place des Lices is another mainstay for Southern Italian fare. “It’s my favorite address for authentic Italian cuisine,” says Cohen.

Where to Stay

One of the best known accommodations in town, Hôtel Byblos has been hosting celebs like Mick Jagger, Cher, and Grace Kelly since it debuted right in the heart of town in the 1960s. The neo-Provençal property, featuring pastel-colored stucco buildings and terracotta tiles, offers 86 rooms and suites decorated in a modern Mediterranean style. It recently updated several rooms along with its onsite food and beverage program, adding three new venues including a gorgeous rooftop bar with high-end cocktails and Champagnes.

A short drive up the hill, five-star Hôtel Lou Pinet offers a vintage, bohemian chic vibe throughout its lobby, restaurant, spa, and 34 rooms. It is anchored by the largest hotel pool in the area, which is surrounded by lush greenery and fragrant native flora like lavender, jasmine, and citrus trees that elevate the property’s regional charm. Book a room here if you want easy access to town via bicycle, foot, or car (including open-air Moke) in a serene, design-forward digs.

Set up in the hills of Gassin, five-star Althoff Villa Belrose offers easy access to all the action of Saint-Tropez but with a serene and quiet vibe. Its 30 modern French provincial-style rooms all boast beautiful marble-clad bathrooms and peaceful terraces with views of the bay or its pretty garden. For large groups, the property also offers three- to six-bedroom villas with access to all the hotel’s amenities, including its cliffside pool. 

For a tranquil beachside retreat, Ferrari highly recommends Lily of The Valley, 30 minutes from Saint-Tropez. Unlike many of the high-end hotels (including our other recommendations), this luxury wellness hotel is open year-round. The Philippe Starck-designed property combines rustic and luxe natural elements, like walnut ceilings and marble bathrooms, throughout the rooms and expansive spa and wellness spaces. “It’s perfect for peace and quiet while having access to the most beautiful beaches in the area,” Ferrari says.

Go full White Lotus at Château de La Messardière. The 19th-century palace turned luxury hotel is the setting for the show’s next season. It features beautiful views of Pampelonne Bay  on a stunning 13-hectare property planted with umbrella pines and cypress trees and beautiful gardens as well as multiple pools, restaurants, and 86 rooms and suites. Production of the show runs through October, so you might even get a chance to see next season’s cast in the flesh.

title: 3 Up-and-Coming Italian Wine Regions You Absolutely Need on Your Radar

Magazine Director Ryan Grim sits down with WE Writers-at-Large for a chat about Bardolino, Maremma, and Mamoiada.

The post 3 Up-and-Coming Italian Wine Regions You Absolutely Need on Your Radar appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
Every summer, we publish an issue all about Italy, and this year’s is a stunner, packed with original photography and reporting from Umbria, Friuli-Venezia Giulia, Valle d’Aosta, Sardinia, and more. The country is always such a joy to cover because it has more native grape varieties than anywhere else in the world, and the diversity of wines produced across its many regions and subregions is truly staggering.

While the famous Italian regions and styles get plenty of love at bottle shops and restaurants, there are so many others that go underappreciated. In this special three-part episode of the Wine Enthusiast Podcast, we dive into under-the-radar Italian wines that most Americans aren’t really drinking—but should be.

Naturally, I solicited the help of the Wine Enthusiast Writers-at-Large who cover Italy for us—Jeff Porter, Danielle Callegari, and Michael Laudenslager—and asked each of them to pick an underrated region. Jeff chose Bardolino, in the Veneto; Danielle went with Tuscany’s Maremma region, which she also covered for the Italy Issue; and Michael picked Mamoiada in Sardinia. All three are exceptional in their own ways, blending compelling histories with bright futures spearheaded by innovative producers—and all of them are criminally under-represented in the United States. Listen to learn more about your new favorite wine regions.

On Why Bardolino Is So Special

Jeff Porter: “The one thing I want to make super clear is it’s an easy wine to drink, but it’s not easy intellectually. It’s fun, but it’s kind of like a band that just popped into my head, like Phoenix or MGMT, or kind of like poppy indie rock that you listen to the first time and you automatically get into it. But then if you spend a little more time with the album or the song, you’re like, ‘Wow, there’s a lot more texture and layers to the production of that song.’ And that’s what that’s what this region is like.”

On How Lago di Garda Affects the Region’s Wines

JP: “It’s in the middle of the country in this area that’s landlocked. [The lake] creates a Mediterranean climate, so it’s warm, and then there are big shifts in temperature. So during the day it can be mid-90s, maybe pushing a hundred, but then it creates this wind because the lake is so big that this wind in the late afternoon cools off a bunch of different areas where the vineyards are and brings the temperature down. So the grapes don’t have to run a marathon or sprint every day. They can just chug along, be hot when it’s hot, and then know they’re gonna be able to rest in the evening and cool off. And that gives you that vibrancy and energy and tension and acidity that I think makes this wine so endearing.”

On Why the Maremma Has Historically Been Underappreciated

Danielle Callegari: “There are a few practical reasons that have led the Maremma to be less loved than other parts of Tuscany. One is that historically it was a swamp that had to be, as the Italians refer to it, ‘requalified.’ Under Mussolini’s fascist regime, they came in and filled in a lot of the swampy areas and made it much more practical for farming and all kinds of agriculture in general. And so it’s, as far as Italy is concerned, a relatively young region for agriculture. It’s also because of its location. It’s not on the Grand Tour trail. So when you’re coming up from Rome, you shoot inwards towards Florence and you kind of skip the Maremma altogether. 

Because of the fact that it wasn’t as easy to work with, it didn’t have great infrastructure, and wasn’t easy to get to. So people kind of just ran right past it, I guess you could say, for a lot of the last century.”

On What Makes Wines from the Tuscan Coast Different

DC: “We don’t think of Tuscany as a place where there are cliffs and sea and lush forests, exactly. So [the Maremma] doesn’t dovetail with expectations, and that makes it exciting to me.

That’s something to spend time on when you’re considering what distinguishes wines from this particular area. The salt air and the shells that are in the soil, which we know that’s true for a lot of Tuscany, but in this area there’s an incredible salinity of freshness.

One thing my friends who make wine there kept pointing out to me was the presence of a consistent wind and that cooling effect that comes off of the water that unites the Maremma with other coastal regions that people are more familiar with, like Bolgheri and Suvereto—which is not particularly famous, but that I think has been appreciated a little bit more. The entire coast of Tuscany has this very different climate because of the sea air, not just for the salty part, which people are really into right now and is kind of a hip, buzzy wine word, but also because of that wind.”

On a Group of Sardinian Winemakers Called the Mamojà

Michael Laudenslager: “There are twenty-five winemakers who created a group inside the Mamoiada, which is the region, called the Mamojà. They’re only gonna work on Grenache, which is Cannonau in that region, and a native white varietal called Granatza, which is not related to Grenache, even though it sounds like it would be. 

They’re making, like, these leaner, fresh, precise styles that are crazy aromatic. And when I say crazy aromatic, I mean they’re really enticing. I don’t want to say ‘Burgundian’—that’s an easy thing to say. I think that word’s thrown around so much, right? What does Burgundian even mean anymore? But they’re interesting aromatics that really grab the attention of a wine drinker.

These are as raw as it comes, which is really great. It’s such a small region, such a small production at the moment. They’re pretty much stainless steel-focused in the beginning of their winemaking, and then it sees time in oak for just resting and aging. But because of that stainless steel fermentation, you are getting a lot of freshness on the nose and on the palate.”

On the Rebellious Spirit of Mamoiada Winemakers

ML: “That was a question I brought up with the winemakers: ‘Do you want to be a DOC?’ And some of them say, ‘Yeah, we would like that because we wanna be recognized,’ but other people right now are enjoying a kind of rebellious nature. It’s drawing attention.

If you look, in the history of winemaking, anytime somebody makes a group or calls themselves a group, really great things happen. Because we’re in Italy, I think the most obvious one is the Barolo Boys. They started getting away from austere, big, powerful—of course, Barolo is still powerful—but away from that old-man stuff that you have to wait for to become a beautiful wine. Another one could be the Gang of Four, in Beaujolais, which really put natural winemaking practices out into the world. They all created groups for themselves to become recognized and become a little rebellious, and it was really great.”

The Guests

Jeff Porter reviews wines from Northern Italy (Piedmont, Lombardy, Liguria, Veneto, Alto Adige, Trentino, Friuli-Venezia Giulia), Central Italy (Emilia-Romagna, Marche & Umbria), Slovenia, and Switzerland. His sommelier career began in Napa Valley, working at Tra Vigne Ristorante. He joined the Bastianich Hospitality Group in 2009 at Osteria Mozza under the auspice of James Beard Award-winning chef Nancy Silverton. Porter then served as the Wine Director at Del Posto Ristorante in NYC and grew to be the Beverage Operations Director for the company.

Danielle Callegari reviews wines from Tuscany (Bolgheri, Chianti Classico, Brunello and Rosso di Montalcino, and the Valdarno), Abruzzo, and Sicily. She is an Associate Professor in the Department of French and Italian at Dartmouth College and Communications Director of the Dante Society of America. Dr. Callegari’s teaching and research focus on premodern Italian literature and food and beverage studies. In addition to her many articles and contributions to academic and trade presses, she is author of Dante’s Gluttons: Food and Society from the Convivio to the Comedy (Amsterdam University Press, 2022) and A Bite-Sized History of Italy (New Press, 2026). 

Michael Laudenslager reviews wines from subregions of Tuscany, Southern Italy, and Sardinia. He is the Wine Director at Respect Hospitality’s restaurant Peasant and a seasoned sommelier with certification from the Court of Master Sommeliers. His career includes managing the beverage programs for renowned chefs Marc Forgione, Peter McAndrew, and Tony Clark; serving as the Director of Restaurants for Marriott International in Washington, D.C. and New York; and curating and pouring wines at the original Smith & Wollensky in New York.

Yeah, so you see it referred to as the wild west of Tuscany. That kind of plays into that sort of like off-the-beaten-path sort of mentality.

DC

I would say that generally I’d really emphasize that the best thing about that or the thing that Maremma most has going for it is this lack of attention, because you go to you know Brunello, you go to Montalcino, you go to Chianti, there’s a lot of history and that also means a lot of baggage, a lot of expectations, a lot of pressure. 

So while in all the other parts of Tuscany there are plenty of young people jumping in and taking over their family properties, or beginning to work together with the older generation, they have to work, you know, inside of certain parameters. With boundaries and guardrails up for sure. And you go to the Maremma, and because there aren’t expectations and there isn’t an already kind of cemented relationship with a certain audience, there’s just a lot more experimentation all around. And I started really paying attention seriously to the area. When I first visited Tancredi Biondi Santi’s property, Castello di Montepò, not least because, as his name announces, there’s a lot of history in his family when it comes to winemaking. And so when I found out that he was working in this other very different space, I was of course already kind of curious, just

in a very general way, what brought someone who had been making wine in the most famous part of Tuscany in the most famous house, probably in all of Italy for a long time, to choose this area and what was he up to? 

It’s not just that he happened to come across this property. It’s something he really believes in. And so when I saw his enthusiasm and excitement about this particular territory, I decided that it was worth digging into. And then right near him is one of my other favorite properties in the area, Fattoria Le Pupille, first made famous a long time ago by Elisabetta Geppetti, who is a woman who absolutely embodies great choices, I think. She’s somebody who’s just tasteful in every way, and her wines always reflect that. And she turned over, much to her credit, she turned over winemaking to her very young son, Ettore, and she remains extremely active in property. 

But I think I understood that the strength of this region was the fact that there were young people here and that they were able to be playful and figure out what was best for them. And Ettore makes really, really elegant wines, but also really unexpected ones. I really fell in love first with the Petit Manseng that he makes, which is to me an icon of this area because it is so unexpected. You’re not going to Tuscany looking for Petit Manseng, obviously. You’re not expecting to find a cru or a clos, in this case, of any white wines really and you’re not expecting to find somebody who really kind of lets it be what it’s going to be without kind of trying to shoehorn it into some predisposed idea and that you know, when I come back to that wine, from Fattoria Le Pupille, I always say to myself, you know, this is like the reward you get for being a little bit intrepid.

RG

So, it’s almost like the lack of the anxiety of influence is one of their greatest sort of, you know, benefits of the region, right?

DC

Hundred percent. And as a literature professor first and foremost, nothing makes me happier than being able to cite Harold Bloom in the course of a podcast.

RG

What are they growing up there other than Sangiovese and Petit Manseng?

DC

Well, there’s really everything. Speaking of people experimenting. And I think, you know, one of the things that’s a challenge for the region right now is trying to get a more coherent identity. So all that experimentation can become a little bit chaotic, even though I find that to be very fun. On the other hand, one thing that you can definitely look for and always find, and that does I think have a kind of a real clarity of vision is their Vermentino. And that’s, as you expect, it’s exactly the kind of grape that will do well under these circumstances. And I think that almost every producer… I just did a big tasting for them. It went along with the writing that I was doing for the magazine at the same time. And I found that the Vermentinos were really where everyone was not necessarily making a showstopper, but was making something super reliable, really delicious, and extremely accessible to almost any consumer, certainly this time of year, a Vermentino is, you know, warm citrus, a little salt, a nice high acid, exactly what you’re looking for in on on a summer afternoon. 

And then from there you can get into all kinds of really special expressions of the so-called international varietals, plenty of people working with Cabernet and Merlot and then you have everything in between. And of course the Sangiovese from the area that’s known colloquially as Morellino is something that has had mixed fortunes. It got really popular for a little while, then it kind of lost some of that traction. But now I think it’s very well positioned because it’s the kind of leaner, fresher, crunchier version of Sangiovese that right now audiences seem to really find themselves in.

RG

In the U.S. at least, what do you think the future holds? Because I know that some of these are pretty reasonably priced wines, what’s their their strategy? Like what are they looking forward to?

DC

I think if they do it right, they can take advantage of the thing that I’m always trying to push, especially Italian producers to really understand, which is that the American audience is without preconceptions. So while Italians see these things about the different regions, either on a grand scale from Tuscany to Piedmont or in a more zoomed in lens, looking at the difference between, for example, Brunello di Montalcino and coastal Tuscany. There they have these understandings of the long history of how wine was produced, of what people expect to have from those areas and whether or not they esteem them because of that. Whereas Americans, of course, are not held back by any of that. So these would be kind of new regions or less loved ones have an opportunity to connect with new incoming drinkers, whatever age they are, who are just finding what they like for the first time. And at the super accessible price point they feel comfortable experimenting and taking a risk. And I think they’ll be delighted with what they find.

RG

Well I think that about covers it. I think we did it. Thanks so much for being here.

DC

It’s been a pleasure as usual, Ryan. Thank you.

RG

So we saved probably the least well known subregion for last, Mamoiada. Writer at large Michael Laudenslager is on the line to talk about this slice of Sardinia.

RG

Hey Michael, thanks for being here. How’s it going?

Michael Laudenslager

Good, Ryan. What’s going on, man? Thanks for having me.

RG

Good. Yeah, we’re here to talk about Mamoiada. Why do you think Mamoiada is underrated, a little underappreciated?

ML

You know what? Because it started as a wine that was really big, macho, high alcohol. You know, the best way to put it for people to understand is like old man wine, you know what I mean? And that’s pretty much who was making those wines for generations. 

RG

Yeah, and where is it in Sardinia and what’s the landscape?

ML

So you’re pretty much smack in the middle of Sardinia, shaded a little to the east pretty much looking at Tuscany. When you’re thinking of Sardinia, I guess everyone’s thinking of beaches, right? The beautiful south is Cagliari and then the Alghero in the north which is like, you know, billionaires and yacht clubs, right?

We’re in the mountains now. Probably not a lot of tourists have been there. It gets pretty high elevation up there too, which we all know high elevation in wine usually leads to a beautiful thing. You get high acidity and a little bit more precision in those wines. And yeah, they’re making some beautiful Grenache or you know, in that region they call it Cannonau.

RG

Yeah, so you wouldn’t call it a touristy area, but a lot of the wineries, you know, they’re accepting visitors and it’s touristy in its own way, or is it kind of too off the beaten path?

ML

Yeah, it’s really off the beaten path. Like when I stayed there, right after VinItaly, I scheduled a trip to go hang with all these winemakers. And there’s not even a hotel. You know, I try to Airbnb, I think there was one. So one of the winemakers, Simone, who’s became a good friend of mine, let me sleep at one of his buddies’ houses, which was pretty cool.

Yeah, there’s really no tourist attraction there. There’s like maybe a couple restaurants, but really what I found is like one restaurant everyone goes to and just so happens that restaurant owner, the husband and wife, make wine for Mamoiada. And then there’s like one enoteca, which is you know, a wine bar, that guy also makes wine for Mamoiada. It’s really cool. It’s like a whole community dedicated to this group of winemakers called the Mamoja.

RG

How much of that’s leaving Sardinia now or is most of it staying there?

ML

Most of it right now is staying there. There’s a pact of like twenty-five winemakers that created the group inside the Mamoiada, which is the region, and then they made a group called the Mamoja, which is a group of twenty-five. They’re only gonna work on Grenache, which is Cannonau in that region, and a native white varietal called Granatza, which is not related to Grenache, even though it sounds like it would be. 

RG

So for people who are familiar with Grenache, how is what they’re doing, you know, different than what you might, you know from Spain or know, even Australia?

ML

You know, here’s the thing. I don’t think it’s that much different from Spain and Australia, where if you go to drink Cannonau in Sardinia, it really is a little different than you know, Spanish Grenache and what you would find in Australia. So what they’re doing, from what it seems like and from talking with them, is really to chase these really great styles that Spain is. Comando G is probably the one of the hottest Grenache wines right now in maybe all the world. And same thing with like the Adelaides in Australia. They’re making like these leaner, fresh, precise styles that are crazy aromatic. And when I say crazy aromatic, I mean like they’re really enticing. They’re really I don’t want to say Burgundian, that’s an easy thing to say. I think that word’s thrown around so much, right? What does Burgundian even mean anymore? But they’re interesting aromatics that really grab the attention of a wine drinker.

RG

So if I was looking for some of these in the U.S., the ones that do make it here, what’s a producer I should be looking for?

ML

You know, there are very few right now in the U.S. The one that I’ve seemed to fall in love with is Vike Vike,  not just because I became close with the guy making the wine, I became close with the guy making the wine because I love his wines, you know? So I kinda had the wine first and then I found the guy. You know, it was one of those stories: I have to find the person that made this wine.

And how I had that wine is funny. I was in Cagliari, which is like a coastal town in Sardinia, me and my girlfriend were going out to dinner, but we had some time before, and we found some really cool historic wine shop and I saw all these Mamoja wines. And at the time I only knew one, and there was this one, Vike Vike, that stood out to me and I was like, that looks cool.

So we bought a bottle of the rosé and we actually just drank it out of the bottle on the way to dinner. And out of the bottle without a wine glass, we were like, wow, this is pretty good. So after that, we started looking all over town for wines. And because you’re in Sardinia, we had access to almost all of them.

RG

The winemaking process, what’s it like in the vineyard? A lot of these are biodynamic, are they organic wineries?

ML

Yeah, these are as raw as it comes, which is really great. You know, it’s such a small region, such a small production at the moment. and they’re just raw wines, you know. They’re pretty much stainless steel focused in the beginning of their winemaking, and then it sees time in oak for you know just resting and aging. But because of that stainless steel fermentation, you are getting a lot of freshness on the nose and on the palate. 

The whole vine system is like bush-trained vines, right? Really sitting low to the ground. They get wind constantly up in that mountainous region because they’re kind of pressed to the east coast and high altitude. So that low-trained vine system is pretty much needed unless they find like a little valley or something that they could plant new vines, which some people have been doing. They also started putting zones on their labels. So there’s a north, there’s an east, a south, a west, and they are distinguishing how different these are, which they are different, just like any other AOC or DOC or DOCG would tell you. It’s a very different composition for each vineyard.

RG

But it’s not a DOC or is it? No, it’s not.

ML

No, it’s not. So this is what’s funny about it, and I really like it. The Mamoja, they’re kind of rebellious, and I think that’s a very important thing in winemaking, right? The DOC for Cannonau di Sardinia is the whole island of Sardinia. Which is kind of crazy, right? Like that really falls into IGT category, if you look anywhere else in Italy.

RG

Yeah.

ML

If you look at a zone that big, it kind of falls into IGT category. So what they’re doing is kind of saying, We don’t want to be a part of that DOC because we’re small, so we should be a DOC. So they’re purposely declassifying it for that reason, and that is why they came up with the group, the Mamoja, because they believe in something new and different.

RG

So in the future they hope to one day have their own?

ML

Yeah, I mean that was a question I brought up with the winemakers. Like, do you want to be a DOC? And some of them say, Yeah, we would like that ’cause we wanna be recognized, but other people right now are enjoying that kind of rebellious nature. It’s kinda drawing attention, which normally, you know, those acts do, you know, they draw attention to people and they’re doing a good job at it.

RG

Yeah, and they kinda just enjoy the complete lack of guardrails. So if they were of a DOC then there’d be other restrictions that would then come about, right?

ML

For sure. Yeah, they would have to put all their and they have rules that they set for themselves inside their own group of twenty five winemakers, which I think is really great, you know. And if you look in the history of winemaking, anytime somebody makes a group or calls themselves a group, really great things happen. I mean, because we’re in Italy, I think the most obvious one is the Barolo boys, right?

RG

Yeah.

ML

So they they started getting away from like that austere, big, powerful, which of course Barolo is still powerful, but that that again, that old man stuff that you have to wait for to become a beautiful wine. Another one could be the Gang of Four, for Beaujolais, which really put natural winemaking practices out into the world.

You know, and they all created groups for themselves to become recognized and become a little rebellious and you know, it was really great.

RG

How are they all working together? Are they sharing fruit? Is it kind of like a co-op?

ML

No, they all have their own vineyards. Yeah, it’s not a co-op. No one’s making wine together or sharing wine. They have vineyards that go back with vine age that are the oldest I found were around eighty-five years old. And then some other people are just finding new places to plant vineyards and they’re not ready yet. 

RG

They all do.

ML

Mamoiada always had vines and there are still some you know old styles that exist there. Yeah, like you know, Montisci which is probably the most historic one, he’s actually in the zone where all these guys are making wine for the Mamoja. And it’s funny, this guy refuses to talk to them really because he thinks that they’re going against the traditional style, which they absolutely are, but in my opinion they’re making better wine for what the world is asking for at the moment.

And not just at the moment. I think these styles of wine are a little bit more with more longevity, you know what I mean? Like think of Burgundy. People love those styles of wine and that’s kinda where we’re going. Like a little lean, fresh, maybe a little bit of tannin, right? But nothing that’s too big and bold and in your face, you know. These are wines that are fun, easy to drink, but l like I said, they’re a lot more exciting and a lot more accessible to drink at the moment. You know, you don’t have to wait a couple years, you can pull the cork now and see what’s in that bottle.

RG

What are the biggest flavors? Like cherry flavors, strawberry, what are we dealing with?

ML

It varies across the board. I would say yeah, you’re definitely getting like a leaner-style cherry flavor. Nothing like black cherry or dark cherry like that. Nothing overripe cherry either. 

Could there be strawberry or those red fruits? Absolutely. I don’t think you’re getting anything that’s gonna be like tart berry or like, you know, like kind of like a bramble berry-type thing or a raspberry or something like that. You’re you’re in the roasted lean fresh cherry world. They’re crushable, but they’re also refined, you know. 

So for me, listen, I get to drink really great wines, you know, and sometimes they are very expensive. I’m not buying them, though, you know what I mean? Not yet in my life, anyway. Hopefully one day I could point at a bottle of DRC and buy it. but that’s not happening, and these wines are falling in that category of price right now where they’re not cheap, but they’re also not expensive. So you could find on a wine list at around like a hundred and thirty to hundred and fifty dollars, where that’s pretty much my price point if I’m looking for a really good bottle of wine.

RG

In the shop, what would they be?

ML

In the shop, you’d probably find them around forty five to fifty dollars, ranging all the way up to around ninety dollars for their high-end Ghirada, which is what they call their cru or their contrada.

RG

And what what’s the white like? What’s the white called again? Yeah, what’s that like?

ML

The white’s Granatza. It’s actually really, really interesting. They could resemble things like Chenin. They could also resemble not burgundy, but they have a little reduction to them like you would find in Burgundy, right? And when I say reduction, just these aromatics that are a little bit more, I don’t know, the best way to say for someone that doesn’t know reduction that are different. 

There’s no oxidative thing happening here, like brown apple type stuff or like applesauce type stuff. But there’s a beautiful reduction on these wines that again, if you’re a serious wine drinker and really into wine, Sardinian Granatza’s really what you want in that category. Yeah they’re they’re pretty high end. They’re cool. And the whole winemaking process there changed a lot because there’s one specific winemaker from a winery called Esole. She went away to the Loire, started making Chenin, and she found some practices there on vine training that was super important for the wine. One thing is like how you arc the vine instead of like you could actually take a vine and just bend it ninety, right? And what you’re doing there is you’re kinda constricting let’s just say flow through the vine, where the arc is actually like you’re you’re kind of forcing a little bit more harder travel, but it’s actually more fluent. And it just a little bit more precision inside the the final juice, you know? That’s something that she learned and brought over to the Mamoja from France.

RG

Well, I think I think we covered it. I could keep talking about Sardinia all day, but I think we gotta wrap it up, man.

ML

Yeah, man. I could talk about it too. It’s something I fell in love with. I fell in love with the region first just for visiting. And then by, you know, by natural discovery, I found these wines and to me I think they’re the most exciting wines right now in Italy. Because it’s a style that you really haven’t seen in Italy yet, and it’s happening in Sardinia, which is pretty cool.

RG

Yeah, I would love some more to make it over here.

ML

Yeah, for sure, man. Well, I appreciate you having me here, man. And anytime you want to talk Italian wine and shop, I’m here for you, brother.

RG

That sounds great. Thanks for hopping on.

RG

And that about does it for this episode. We have three fascinating Italian regions that really should be on your radar if they aren’t already. Check out more from Italy in the 2026 Italy issue in print and online at wineenthusiast.com. Send us your comments and questions at podcast@ wineenthusiast.com. Subscribe to this podcast on Apple, Spotify, and anywhere else you listen to your favorite shows. You can also go to wineenthusiast.com/podcast for more episodes and transcripts. I’m Ryan Grim, thanks for listening.

Designed to Shine: The Italian Prosecco That Doubles as a Statement Piece

Whether you’re planning a milestone celebration or simply gathering a small group of friends for an impromptu dinner party, the details can feel overwhelming. There’s a menu to set, a table to shape, a guest list to curate, and, of course, drinks to pour.

Choosing a bottle that looks like it belongs at the table adds to that convivial feeling, which is why Brilla!, premium Italian Prosecco is the preferred choice for so many hosts.

Combining authentic Italian craftsmanship with modern style, Brilla! Prosecco DOC Rosé and Prosecco DOC are an effortless choice to pair alongside classic entertaining fare, from freshly shucked oysters to shrimp cocktail to charcuterie. 

With a delicate and complex bouquet of pear, green apple, and lemon as well as floral notes of acacia and rose, the Rosé is fresh and light on the palate, with balanced acidity and body.

Made from Prosecco’s iconic white grape, Glera, known for producing light-bodied, high-acid wines with neutral to fruit-forward aromatics, along with Pinot Noir, the blend offers a round and full-bodied structure. This makes it perfect to enjoy as an aperitif, but also positions it as an ideal accompaniment to Prosciutto e Melone (Cured Ham & Cantaloupe) and grilled fish entrées.

Meanwhile, the crisp and dry profile of the Prosecco DOC feels fresh on the palate, with balanced acidity and body.

The pronounced peach and green apple notes set the tone for a decadent evening of al fresco summer dinners and pair impeccably with seasonal favorites likegrilled chicken and peaches. And the iconic sound of popping open a bottle only prolongs guests’ desire to linger at the table for hours, talking long after the meal is complete. 

Don’t be surprised if Brilla!’s distinctive, jewel-inspired bottle design comes up as a topic. The conversation-starting, covetable object reflects the meaning of the Italian word (“to shine”). It’s the ideal choice for hosts who understand that the eyes eat first, and that the style of a tablescape influences how guests feel about the menu, the company, and the celebration to come. 

“Brilla was designed to stand apart long before the first pour,” says a representative from the brand. “Its distinctive patented textured bottle, inspired by the brilliance of cut crystal, transforms every bottle into a statement piece—reflecting the sparkle, elegance, and celebration found inside.”

The Brilla! bottle is the result of a design study that goes beyond a simple wine bottle. Its patented texture is reminiscent of a diamond, and echoes a classic gemstone drop shape.

In the world of diamonds, drop-shaped stones are among the most distinctive and difficult to craft; the symmetry, which is achieved with hard work and dedication during processing, is key to the overall beauty of this stone.

Worn as a ring, earring, or pendant, the shape provides a characteristic elegance with which no other diamond cut can compete; it enhances, romantically and gently, the wearer’s form.

This makes each bottle an effortless gift, requiring no additional gift wrap or presentation.

As a natural bridge between the worlds of fashion, design, and hospitality, Brilla! is a beloved choice for making celebratory, Prosecco-based cocktails, which can signal the start of a brunch or aperitif hour in style.

Some of the most common and popular examples include the Aperol Spritz, Bellini, Mimosa, and Negroni Sbagliato, with Prosecco.

In each of these cocktails, Brilla! adds a layer of sophistication and complexity, and sets the tone for an elevated, elegant occasion that guests will associate with a design-minded host.

title: Was the Wine Industry Worrying About the Wrong Generation?
summary:
New data debunks the myth that Gen Z is drinking less. Baby boomers, on the other hand, are a different story.

The post Was the Wine Industry Worrying About the Wrong Generation? appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
Key Points

  • Gen Z alcohol consumption has climbed to 74%, debunking early fears that younger adults are abstaining entirely.
  • Conversely, Baby Boomers show the steepest drop in alcohol consumption, becoming the true generation of moderation.
  • Younger consumers prioritize social experiences and higher quality drinks over traditional wine cellaring or heavy drinking.

The wine industry can breathe easy. According to a newly-released report from beverage analytics firm IWSR, the alcohol consumption rate amongst Gen Z has risen to 74%, up from 66% three years ago. 

After all the hand-wringing about whether this generation, which includes people born between 1996 and 2010, would ever come around to drinking, the stats are showing that they are. More than 84% of Gen Z (of legal drinking age) have consumed cocktails in the last six months, which is more than any other generation. Gen Z has the second-highest beverage alcohol participation rate (77%) of any generation, slightly behind Millennials. 

“The industry spent a long time asking whether younger consumers were interested in wine, when the more interesting question was why it didn’t seem like they were,” says Tynan Pierce, the wine director at Yes Society, the wine club founded by Antica Terra’s Maggie Harrison. “I don’t think younger drinkers were rejecting wine. I think they were rejecting the way wine was being presented to them.”

Baby boomers, however, are a different story. According to the report, boomers (ages 62 to 80) registered significant declines across all consumption metrics. That demographic—long a stronghold for wine sales—has the lowest consumption rate of any generation. 

While the industry has been fretting about Gen Z sales, a key generation was aging out of wine. Have wine pros been worrying about the wrong generation?

The Kids Are Alright

The good news is that 20-somethings are spending money in the alcohol sector. Sure, wine is splitting sales with ready-to-drink cocktails, coolers, and the like, but they’re not vaping instead or abstaining entirely, as early reports suggested.

“The narrative that Gen Z is the generation of moderation is now conclusively debunked,” says IWSR President and Managing Director Marten Lodewijks.

However, as the IWSR report points out, this young generation is interacting with alcohol differently than their elders did.

For one, Gen Z is a cocktail crowd—84% have consumed cocktails in the last six months. They center alcohol around occasions: 18% reported that their last drink was enjoyed in the context of gatherings with five or more people (so, parties.)

Drew Brady, wine director at Ravi DeRossi’s Long Count (and one of Wine Enthusiast’s 2023 Future 40), has noticed that what Gen Z lacks in drinking culture knowledge, they make up for with a love of events, nights out, and occasions. “It feels like drinking is less of an automatic part of the week—the way it was for us—and more attached to a chosen night out,” Brady says. “

While they may not be collecting as much, or spending in the same way, Gen Z is proving to be particularly appreciative of some of wine’s best qualities—storytelling and connection. 

“They want to know who made the wine, how it was made, and why it works on the menu,” he says. “How does this contribute to their experience? A bottle does not need to be famous, but it does need to feel alive, distinctive, and worth remembering.”

“The biggest shift we’re seeing is from accumulation to curation,” says Tyson. “Previous generations often viewed wine through the lens of building a cellar, while younger consumers tend to view wine as something to be opened, shared, and experienced.”

A recent study funded by Bacardi seconded this, finding that Gen Z tends to drink earlier in the day rather than late at night, at occasions rooted around socializing. The Bacardi report also found that 70% of emotionally engaged consumers will spend twice as much on brands they connect with.

“Gen Z is not necessarily rejecting alcohol,” says Charles Ewudo, founder and CEO of PCN Entertainment, a nightlife giant spanning clubs, cocktail bars, and drinks brands. “They are rejecting outdated ways of discovering and engaging with brands … The alcohol industry has viewed Gen Z’s changing relationship with drinking as a challenge, but I think it’s important to recognize that Gen Z is also showing brands where the future of consumer behavior is headed.”

The IWSR’s Lodewijks confirms this: “While Gen Z consumers are creating new patterns for engaging with beverage alcohol, the evidence demonstrates that Gen Z consumers enjoy drinking at roughly the same levels as the rest of society.”

OK, Boomer

While the kids are alright, the IWSR’s report flagged that boomers are not. Drinking continues to decline among the demographic. Boomers reported the smallest number of drinking occasions of any generational cohort and reported consuming the smallest number of drinks when they do drink (an average of 2.6 drinks per occasion). 

“Boomer drinking has been tailing off for several years,” says Lodewijks. This is unsurprising for consumers hitting their 60s and 70s—people grow older, health goals shift.

“These latest Bevtrac results, however, show bigger-than-expected drops in boomer drinking across all major metrics,” he continues. “If this trend continues, it may actually be the boomers, not Gen Z, who deserve the title ‘generation of moderation.”

Moderation Moment

Adding to the fuddle of this all, a global moderation movement has impacted how all demographic groups interact with alcohol. 

49% of Gen Z drinkers reported they are likely to listen to government health guidelines. While consumption rates are steady across all generations, frequency of occasion and amount consumed on each occasion are down—3.9 drinks per occasion, down from 4.4 drinks in 2025.

Thankfully, this reflects a general shift towards a less-but-better approach to alcohol consumption. Last year’s IWSR BevTrac report noted that Gen Z consumers buy less, but do spend more when they make a purchase.

“Gen Z is not consuming mass quantities at the low end, and instead drinking higher quality wines,” says Tim Willard, partner at wine bar Madeira Park. “This generation seems undaunted by the mystery of wine—their comfort zone is exponentially larger than previous generations.”

He finds his restaurant is a playground for all generations, so he gets a front-row seat to the way people actually engage with wine. 

“I think the most important shift is Gen Z’s attitude on quality with little regard for the appellation system,” he says. “It’s actually having a bottom-up effect on older generations, who seem more open to trying wine from less familiar-to-them grapes and places.”

The Takeaway

Is the fact that boomers are spending less on wine a reason to panic? Not likely. This generational shift reflects a changing of a guard, a signal of where big wine powers should shift focus towards. 

“Boomers have historically been some of the most loyal alcohol consumers, but loyalty does not mean immunity to shifting behaviors,” says Ewudo. “As this generation gets older, health, wellness, lifestyle changes, and moderation are impacting consumption habits.”

In short? “The industry cannot assume that yesterday’s loyal customer will consume the same way tomorrow. “
